coverage.rule: A test row is counted at the whole percent nearest to the oxygen it states (20.95% counts at 21%). Only a row that states one oxygen value for its atmosphere can be placed.

not_placed.why: the table has no oxygen column
inverse flames: the oxygen stated is that of the injected gas, not of the atmosphere
one cell lists several oxygen values (a test matrix, not one test in each row)
the oxygen cell of the row is empty

note: Each gap is measured from NASA's tables as fetched for this site. Plans are quoted from NASA pages and reports in the ledger.
outside_note: Returned by another fire-related search of PSI but not by the combustion search, so not among the records on this site.

items.title: No row in PSI's tables was taken in lunar or Martian gravity
items.why: Buoyant flow grows with gravity, and the flow near a small flame on the Moon falls where solids burn most readily. Free-fall data bound that case from one side and 1 g data from the other.

evidence.text: Every record in PSI's combustion search is a flight experiment in free fall or ground work. No table row was taken in partial gravity.
Simple scaling puts the buoyant flow near a small flame in lunar gravity at about 6 to 11 cm/s: inside the range the guide calls most flammable. A bound from a formula, not a measurement.

plans.name: FM2, Flammability of Materials on the Moon

items.quote: FM2 is the first-ever combustion experiment to be performed on another planetary body
The experiment burns four fuel samples individually in atmospheric conditions planned for future lunar habitats or vehicles
items.source: NASA Glenn: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)

items.quote: The first-ever combustion experiments on another world will be performed, with a planned launch date of late 2026.
items.source: Ferkul, Kralik and Liao, Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, extended abstract, NTRS 20260000646

items.text: NASA's plan for the Moon, from its 2026 presentation: 4 tests of one fabric at 8.2 psia, starting at 37, 33, 29 and 25% oxygen.
PSI's search for "FM2" returns no record.

items.quote: These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity
items.source: Ferkul et al., Lunar Combustion Investigation: Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket, NTRS 20250010653 (abstract)

items.text: NASA's LUCI flight, in simulated lunar gravity: the flame base on the fabric moved at 0.9 mm/s, against 1.5 mm/s in the same test on Earth. Slower, and it burned longer. Read from NASA's slides; the data are not in PSI.

items.quote: 1-g extinction happens ~ 45 seconds sooner than partial-g extinction
items.source: Ferkul et al., Lunar Combustion Investigation: Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket, presentation, NTRS 20250010653

items.quote: the available times are too short to provide significant flame development (5 s for drop tower and ~25 s for aircraft)
items.source: Ferkul, Kralik and Liao, Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, extended abstract, NTRS 20260000646

items.text: PSI's search for "LUCI" returns no record. Its results are in a NASA presentation, not in the data repository.

items.title: No solid material is on record at a known pressure
items.why: Cabins are built of solids. Exploration cabins trade pressure for oxygen, and the solid-fuel tables in PSI give oxygen alone.

evidence.text: BASS-II and Saffire list oxygen for 140 rows and pressure for none, so none can be placed on the atmosphere map.

items.title: No solid-material row states more than 22.2% oxygen
items.unit: is the most oxygen any of the 140 solid-material rows states
items.why: The two exploration atmospheres on this site's map hold 30% and 34% oxygen, and a suit holds pure oxygen. The solid-fuel rows in PSI run from 13.6% to 22.2%.

evidence.text: Of 887 rows that state oxygen, 140 are solid materials; their oxygen runs from 13.6% to 22.2%. Droplet rows reach 34% and gas-flame rows 40%. No row of any kind states more than 40%.

evidence.quote: The glovebox is normally limited to ISS “air,” nominally 21 percent oxygen by volume and one atmospheric pressure

plans.name: Saffire IV to VI
plans.state: flown; in a paper, not in PSI

items.text: NASA's paper on Saffire IV to VI lists 5 large burns of solid materials at 22% to 31% oxygen and 54.1 to 100 kPa. These tests are not in a PSI table.

items.title: Few tests sit near the atmospheres planned for exploration
items.unit: of 746 rows lie near 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia and 34% at 8.2 psia
items.why: Those rows are liquid droplets and gas flames. Near a suit atmosphere, pure oxygen at 4.3 psia, there are 0.

evidence.text: 215 rows lie near the cabin air of the space station; the count falls to 8 and 11 at the two exploration atmospheres (near means within 0.03 in oxygen fraction and 15% in pressure).

plans.name: FLARE, Flammability Limits at Reduced-g Experiment

items.quote: a new fire safety standard test method for screening spacecraft materials will be proposed that addresses the shortcomings of existing standard test method such as NASA STD 6001B
items.source: NASA Glenn: Flammability Limits at Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE)

items.quote: If proven for more materials, this may indicate the need to include a factor of safety on 1g flammability limits
items.says: Olson and Ferkul, on why the standard needs a second look
items.source: Olson and Ferkul, Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test, NTRS 20130010991

items.title: Most tables say what was set, fewer say what happened
items.unit: of 20 records with a table have an outcome column
items.why: A table of conditions lets a reader find a test. Only an outcome lets a reader learn from it without opening the raw files, which for some records run to terabytes.

evidence.text: Records whose table carries an outcome such as extinction, burn time, burn length or ignition: ACME BRE, ACME CLD Flame, ACME E-FIELD Flames, ACME s-Flame, FLEX, SAFFIRE-I, SAFFIRE-II, SAME-R, SPICE, ACME CFI-G.
BASS-II in PSI: 129 test rows, with oxygen at the start between 13.6% and 22.2%. The table records conditions and gas readings. It has no column saying whether each flame went out.

items.text: One outcome column per experimental table (extinguished, burned out, flow at extinction) would turn the test matrices into data. It is the first line of the report for the PSI curators.

items.title: Half of the large-fire flights are in the repository
items.unit: of six Saffire flights are in PSI
items.why: Saffire burned samples a metre long in a cargo vehicle, the only spacecraft-scale fire data there is.

evidence.text: PSI's search for "Saffire" returns 3 records: PSI-100 (SAFFIRE-III), PSI-98 (SAFFIRE-I), PSI-99 (SAFFIRE-II).

evidence.quote: These tests spanned 1.5 to 3.2 kW with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters
evidence.says: The scale of the later flights
evidence.source: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, NTRS 20240002981 (abstract)

evidence.quote: Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
evidence.source: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, NTRS 20240002981 (abstract)

items.text: Their results are in NASA reports (one is in this site's ledger, NTRS 20240002981). The data sets are not in PSI.

In the two acrylic tests of Saffire VI, carbon monoxide at the far sensors rose by 308 and 320 ppm and carbon dioxide by 3.51 and 3.37 mmHg. NASA's limits in the same paper: 100 ppm of carbon monoxide for 24 hours, 425 ppm for one hour, 3 mmHg of carbon dioxide as a one-hour average. The highest temperature at the far sensors was 21 and 21 °C.

items.quote: Further work will be needed to extend these results to the partial gravity environment expected on future mission to the moon and Mars.
items.source: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, ICES-2024-365, NTRS 20240002981
